items.stem: A department buys a server for ₱180,000 and uses it for four years. A second department rents equivalent capacity and pays ₱3,000 each month. How does accounting record each?

options.text: The purchase is CapEx, an asset depreciated over years. The rental is OpEx, an expense each month.
options.feedback: Owning creates an asset whose cost is spread over its useful life. Renting creates a monthly expense for what was used.

options.text: Both are operational expenditure, because both pay for the same kind of equipment.
options.feedback: The classification depends on whether you own an asset. The type of asset does not matter.

options.text: The purchase is expensed in full in year one, and the rental is depreciated over four years.
options.feedback: This reverses the treatment. Purchases are capitalized, and rental payments are expensed.

options.text: Both are capital expenditure, because both give the department the same computing power.
options.feedback: Rented capacity is not an asset the department owns, so it is an operating expense.

items.stem: You buy capacity above the highest peak of the year, at 320 units. What do the idle-capacity and turned-away figures show?

options.text: Almost nobody is turned away, but most of the capacity you paid for sits unused.
options.feedback: Capacity sized for a brief peak is idle for the rest of the year. The widget shows about 87% unused and nothing turned away.

options.text: Nobody is turned away and almost none of the capacity is wasted.
options.feedback: Demand is quiet for most of the year, so capacity sized for the peak is mostly idle.

options.text: Some demand is still turned away, because demand varies from year to year.
options.feedback: In this chart the demand curve is fixed, and 320 units is above its highest point.

options.text: The year costs less than renting, because buying is cheaper per unit.
options.feedback: Buying for the peak costs several times more than renting the same shape of demand.

items.stem: At 120 units the chart shows both idle capacity and demand turned away in the same year. Why can no single fixed capacity avoid both?

options.text: Demand spikes briefly, so capacity sized for the spikes sits idle for the rest of the year.
options.feedback: A flat line cannot match a spiky curve. Raising the line removes the lost demand and increases the idle capacity.

options.text: The slider range is too small to reach a setting where both problems disappear.
options.feedback: The slider reaches the highest peak, and at that setting nothing is turned away but most capacity is idle.

options.text: Idle capacity means the servers were configured incorrectly for this demand.
options.feedback: The servers work correctly. The idle capacity comes from the shape of demand.

options.text: Rented servers are always cheaper per unit, so buying is a mistake at any setting.
options.feedback: Renting costs more per unit. It wins because you pay only for what you use.

items.stem: A server costs ₱180,000 to buy. Select all that apply: which of these belong in its total cost of ownership?

options.text: Electricity and cooling for as long as it runs.
options.feedback: Operating costs run every hour whether or not anyone uses the system.

options.text: The cost of the system being unavailable during an outage.
options.feedback: Downtime is part of the total cost, and for enlistment morning it can be the largest item.

options.text: Safe disposal of the hardware and its data at the end of its life.
options.feedback: Disposal is a real cost that is usually left out of the original business case.

options.text: The monthly bill for a cloud server you decided not to use.
options.feedback: This is the price of the alternative. It is used for comparison and is not a cost of owning this server.
